lead: Multimedia security protects a photo, audio clip or video from copying, editing and false claims about origin. It exists because one share can reach millions in seconds. Four goals are separate: confidentiality hides content, integrity proves no change, authenticity proves who made it, and ownership proves who owns it. Watermarks, hashes and signatures serve different goals, so one tool cannot do all four. Forensics works backwards from a suspect file to evidence. You meet it in CCTV checks, insurance claims, newsroom verification and leaked paper images.
prereq: You need: image formats and lossy compression from Unit 4, and feature vectors from 6.3.

sections.h3: Four goals and three kinds of mark

blocks.text: Confidentiality hides content. Symmetric encryption uses one shared key; asymmetric encryption uses a public key and a private key. Integrity proves the bits did not change. Authenticity proves who made the file. Ownership proves who owns the media. Encryption gives confidentiality only; it does not prove origin after decryption.

A watermark is a mark embedded in cover media, the original image, audio or video. The marked output is sent to users. Steganography hides the existence of a message. Fingerprinting embeds a different mark in each copy, so a leak can be traced to one recipient.

items: Watermark: ownership proof or tamper check.
Steganography: secret message whose existence is hidden.
Fingerprint: unique mark per recipient for leak tracing.

sections.h3: Embedding a mark: LSB and DCT

blocks.text: An 8-bit pixel holds a value from 0 to 255. Its least significant bit (LSB) is the bit with weight 1. Changing it alters the value by at most 1, so the eye rarely sees the change.

items: Convert the mark to a bit stream.
For each chosen pixel, replace bit 0 with one message bit.
Record the pixel positions and the key.
At the detector, read bit 0 and rebuild the mark.

blocks.text: LSB embedding has high capacity and low robustness. Resaving as JPEG, cropping or scaling destroys it. DCT embedding works on 8×8 blocks. Transform pixels to frequency coefficients, change mid-frequency coefficients, then inverse transform. JPEG also quantises DCT coefficients, so the mark survives ordinary compression better.
MSE = (1/N) Σ (x<sub>i</sub> − y<sub>i</sub>)² ; PSNR = 10 log₁₀(MAX² ÷ MSE)
blocks.where: N is the number of pixels in the block or image; x<sub>i</sub> is the original pixel value; y<sub>i</sub> is the marked pixel value; MAX is the peak value, 255 for 8-bit images; MSE is in squared pixel levels; PSNR is in decibels (dB).

blocks.text: Capacity, robustness and imperceptibility pull against each other. More hidden bits means more change. A stronger mark means visible artefacts. PSNR above about 40 dB usually means the change is invisible for 8-bit images.

A cryptographic hash maps a file to a fixed digest. Any bit change gives a different digest with very high probability. Store the digest; later recompute and compare. A digital signature signs the digest with a private key; anyone with the public key verifies it. This detects edits but does not hide content.
Forensics works backwards from a suspect file to evidence. Follow these steps.

items: Read metadata: camera model, time, GPS and software edits.
Look for copy-move: the same texture or object pasted twice inside one image.
Look for resave traces: JPEG block patterns and double compression.
Keep chain of custody: log every person, time and hash from seizure to court.

blocks.text: The same evidence pipeline appears in 6.8, where cameras produce media faster than people can watch.

figure.caption: Each message bit replaces bit 0 of one pixel, so only 150 changes (to 151); the squared errors are 1, 0, 0. With MSE = 1/3 ≈ 0.333, PSNR = 10 log₁₀(255² ÷ 1/3) ≈ 52.9 dB.

spec.title: LSB embedding of bits 1, 0, 1
spec.aria: A five-row table over three pixels: original values 150, 152, 155, their bit 0 values 0, 0, 1, the message bits 1, 0, 1, the new values 151, 152, 155, and squared errors 1, 0, 0, with the changed pixel 151 and its error 1 highlighted.

examples.question: An 8-bit grayscale image has three pixels with values 150, 152 and 155. Hide bits 1, 0, 1 in the least significant bit of each pixel. Find the new pixel values, the mean squared error over these three pixels, and the PSNR. Use MAX = 255.
steps: Pixel 150 is even, so its bit 0 is 0. Set bit 0 to 1: 150 → 151. Squared error = (150 − 151)² = 1.
Pixel 152 is even, so its bit 0 is 0. Set bit 0 to 0: 152 → 152. Squared error = 0.
Pixel 155 is odd, so its bit 0 is 1. Set bit 0 to 1: 155 → 155. Squared error = 0.
examples.answer: New pixels are 151, 152 and 155; MSE = 1/3 ≈ 0.333 in squared pixel levels; PSNR ≈ 52.9 dB.
examples.check:
import math
px = [150, 152, 155]
bits = [1, 0, 1]
new = [(p & ~1) | b for p, b in zip(px, bits)]
for v in new:
    print(v)
mse = sum((p - n) ** 2 for p, n in zip(px, new)) / len(px)
psnr = 10 * math.log10(255 ** 2 / mse)
print(round(mse, 3))
print(round(psnr, 1))

traps: Using 20 log₁₀ in PSNR. PSNR uses 10 log₁₀ because it is a power ratio; 20 log₁₀ belongs to amplitude ratios such as voltage gain.
Averaging squared error only over changed pixels. MSE divides by N, all pixels in the block or image.
Calling any hidden mark a watermark. Steganography hides existence; fingerprinting traces a recipient; watermarking usually proves ownership or tamper.
Saying a hash encrypts the file. A hash is a one-way digest, not encryption; it detects change but does not hide content.
Expecting LSB marks to survive JPEG. Lossy compression and scaling erase LSB; DCT-domain marks are more robust.

quiz.q: Name the four separate goals of multimedia security.
State one difference between watermarking and fingerprinting.
quiz.a: A watermark usually carries one mark for ownership or tamper checks. Fingerprinting embeds a different mark in each copy, so a leaked copy can be traced to one recipient.

quiz.q: Pixels 100, 101 and 102 carry bits 1, 0 and 1 in their least significant bits. Find the new pixel values, MSE and PSNR with MAX = 255.
Why does DCT-domain embedding survive JPEG better than LSB embedding?
quiz.a: JPEG quantises DCT coefficients, and a mid-frequency DCT mark is changed in the same transform domain. LSB embedding lives in exact pixel values, and quantisation and resaving alter those low bits.

quiz.q: How does a digital signature detect a change in a media file?
quiz.a: The signer signs a hash digest with a private key. The verifier recomputes the digest and checks the signature with the public key. A changed file gives a different digest, so verification fails.

quiz.q: A marked image has MSE = 4 in squared pixel levels. Find PSNR with MAX = 255.
Why does a forensic report need both a hash log and a chain-of-custody record?
quiz.a: The hash log proves the file bits did not change. The chain-of-custody record proves who handled the file, when, and through which transfers. Together they connect the court copy to the seized original.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry now uses content credentials and signed provenance for news photos and AI-generated images. Robust watermarking for generated media is an active research area. Deepfake forensics combines visual artefacts, audio-visual mismatch and metadata. Search for C2PA, perceptual hashing, PRNU camera fingerprinting and double JPEG compression.
